name: Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
populations: people with heavy lifting or prolonged sitting exposure
summary: Displacement of disc material through a fissured annulus, usually posterolaterally at L4–5 or L5–S1, irritating a nerve root and causing leg-dominant pain. Most cases settle without surgery.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve with non-surgical care; 95% of trial patients reported recovery at 1 year, with or without early surgery

keyFacts.label: Natural history
keyFacts.value: Herniations often resorb: pooled 70.4% overall, higher for extrusion and sequestration

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Straight leg raise (pooled sensitivity 0.92, specificity 0.28 in surgical samples); crossed SLR specificity 0.90

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI only if surgery or injection is planned, or red flags are present; protrusions are seen in 29–43% of pain-free adults

keyFacts.label: Red flag
keyFacts.value: Cauda equina syndrome is a same-day emergency

overview:
A lumbar disc herniation is displacement of disc material (nucleus pulposus or annulus fibrosus) beyond the intervertebral disc space. When the displaced material irritates or compresses a lumbar or sacral nerve root it produces radiculopathy, usually felt as leg-dominant pain (sciatica). The highest prevalence is among people aged 30 to 50 years, with a male to female ratio of about 2:1 [r1]. In clinical teaching, most symptomatic herniations occur at L4–5 and L5–S1, the levels enrolled in recent surgical trials [r2].

A herniation on imaging is not the same as a painful herniation. Disc protrusion is present in 29% of pain-free 20-year-olds and 43% of pain-free 80-year-olds, and disc bulge in 30% and 84% respectively [r3]. The diagnosis therefore rests on a radicular history and examination that match the imaging, not on the scan alone.

The natural history is favourable. In a meta-analysis of 31 studies of conservatively treated herniations, 70.4% showed spontaneous resorption (87.8% of sequestrations, 66.9% of extrusions, 37.5% of protrusions and 13.3% of bulges), mostly within 6 months [r4]. Surgery gives faster relief of leg pain in severe sciatica but not a better outcome at 1 year [r5], although it was superior at 6 months for sciatica that had already lasted 4 to 12 months [r2]. The physiotherapist's job is to screen for the minority who need urgent surgical care, and otherwise to educate, keep the person active and rebuild load tolerance.

epidemiology.text: Herniated lumbar disc is most prevalent in people aged 30 to 50 years, with a male to female ratio of 2:1 [r1]. Low back pain in general is most often reported by people with physically demanding jobs, physical or mental comorbidities, smokers and people with obesity [r6]; these data are for low back pain as a whole rather than herniation specifically.

intrinsic: Pre-existing disc degeneration and annular fissuring; both are common and often painless [r3]
Obesity and physical or mental comorbidity (risk factors for low back pain in general) [r6]
extrinsic: Repetitive or sustained lumbar flexion under load, the pattern that produced herniation in a laboratory disc model [r7]
Physically demanding work with heavy or repeated lifting [r6]
Smoking (a risk factor for low back pain in general) [r6]
Prolonged slouched sitting and sudden unprepared loading (common clinical association; not tested in the sources reviewed)

mechanism.summary: Repeated or sustained lumbar flexion combined with compressive load, often with some axial rotation, increases tensile strain on the posterior and posterolateral annulus while the nucleus is squeezed backwards. Cumulative loading creates annular fissures, the nucleus tracks outward along them and eventually pushes through the outer annulus toward the spinal canal or foramen, where it contacts a nerve root.
sequence: The person lifts, lowers or bends repeatedly with a flexed lumbar spine (a stoop lift), or holds a loaded flexed posture for a prolonged period.
Flexion closes the front of the disc and opens the back, so the nucleus is pushed posteriorly and the posterior annular fibres are stretched.
Repeated cycles, with the compressive load of the trunk and the object lifted, create radial and concentric fissures in the posterior and posterolateral annulus.
Nucleus material migrates along a fissure toward the periphery (annular fissure, then nucleus migration).
The disc bulges, protrudes or extrudes beyond the posterior margin, most often posterolaterally where the posterior longitudinal ligament is thinnest.
In the lateral recess the herniation presses on the traversing root (L5 for an L4–5 posterolateral herniation); a foraminal herniation affects the exiting root.
Mechanical compression and the inflammatory chemistry of nucleus material combine to produce radicular pain, paraesthesia and, if compression is severe, weakness.
Over weeks to months macrophages and new vessels remove extruded material and symptoms usually settle.

variants.name: Loaded flexion with rotation
variants.description: Combining loaded flexion with twisting is widely regarded as a high-risk combination for the posterolateral annulus, for example when lifting and turning. This is clinical teaching and was not directly tested in the human studies reviewed.

variants.name: Sudden unprepared load
variants.description: A single event such as lifting while twisting, a fall or a cough or sneeze can be the final straw on an already fissured disc. The person recalls an event, but the structural change has often developed over a longer period.

variants.name: Gradual onset without a clear event
variants.description: Many people with radiculopathy cannot recall a precipitating event. Sitting-related provocation and a slow progression of back pain to leg pain are common.

variants.name: Far-lateral and foraminal herniation
variants.description: These affect the exiting root at that level (for example L4 for an L4–5 foraminal herniation) rather than the traversing root. They cause more thigh and shin pain, may be missed on routine MRI slices and tend to cause more severe pain.

anatomy.text: The lumbar intervertebral disc has a gelatinous, water-rich nucleus pulposus surrounded by concentric lamellae of the annulus fibrosus, which are bounded above and below by cartilaginous endplates. The posterior annulus is covered by the posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL), which is strongest in the midline, so herniations tend to emerge posterolaterally. The traversing nerve root leaves the thecal sac, runs through the lateral recess beneath the superior articular process and exits at the foramen of the level below; the exiting root passes through the foramen at the level of the disc. A posterolateral herniation at L4–5 therefore usually compresses the traversing L5 root, and one at L5–S1 compresses S1. The multifidus and erector spinae stabilise and extend the segment, and the facet joints limit flexion, rotation and shear.

structures.name: Nucleus pulposus
structures.role: Hydrated, proteoglycan-rich core that distributes compressive load and resists deformation

structures.name: Annulus fibrosus
structures.role: Concentric collagen lamellae that contain the nucleus and resist tension, torsion and shear; the posterior and posterolateral region is the usual site of failure

structures.name: Posterior longitudinal ligament
structures.role: Reinforces the posterior annulus centrally and is thinner laterally

structures.name: Traversing and exiting nerve roots
structures.role: Carry motor and sensory fibres; the dorsal root ganglion sits in the foramen and is sensitive to mechanical and chemical irritation

structures.name: Facet (zygapophyseal) joints
structures.role: Limit flexion, axial rotation and anterior shear, and share compressive load, especially in extension

structures.name: Multifidus and erector spinae
structures.role: Segmental and global extensor control of the lumbar spine; guard reflexively in acute pain

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Herniation is a failure of the annulus under combined flexion and compression. In porcine motion segments, herniation of the posterior and posterolateral annulus occurred with relatively modest compression but highly repetitive flexion–extension, and higher compression produced more frequent and more severe injuries [r7]. This is an in-vitro model using cervical segments, so it supports a mechanism of cumulative fatigue failure rather than proving the lumbar human pathway. A classic biomechanical paper framed disc prolapse as a hyperflexion injury [r8].

Pain does not simply track the size of the herniation. A review of the pathophysiology argues for a chemical component acting together with mechanical compression: disc surgery does not consistently relieve pain, large herniations are not always symptomatic, symptom severity and neurological signs correlate poorly with herniation size, and conservative treatment is often effective [r9]. Proinflammatory substances released by the nucleus pulposus, with tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) the leading candidate, are thought to sensitise a nerve root that is also mechanically deformed [r9]. Herniated tissue that shrinks on conservative care shows more neovascularisation and macrophage infiltration, which is the likely mechanism of spontaneous resorption [r10]. Herniations that contain a lot of cartilaginous endplate material, as in discs with Modic changes, contain less nucleus and fewer macrophages and vessels, and resorb poorly [r10].

structures.name: Annulus fibrosus
structures.effect: Radial and concentric fissures in the posterior and posterolateral lamellae allow nucleus migration; the outer annulus may remain intact (protrusion) or be breached (extrusion)

structures.name: Nucleus pulposus
structures.effect: Displaced posteriorly; extruded material may migrate cranially or caudally or separate as a free fragment (sequestration)

structures.name: Traversing nerve root
structures.effect: Compressed in the lateral recess and exposed to nucleus-derived inflammatory mediators, producing radicular pain and, with sustained compression, conduction block

structures.name: Dorsal root ganglion
structures.effect: Particularly sensitive to mechanical and chemical irritation; ectopic discharge contributes to pain and paraesthesia

structures.name: Vertebral endplates
structures.effect: Cartilaginous endplate material can herniate with the nucleus, and Modic changes mark discs that resorb poorly [r10]

muscles.name: Multifidus and erector spinae
muscles.effect: Reflex guarding and spasm in the acute phase; a lateral shift or antalgic posture is common. Local multifidus inhibition with prolonged pain is clinically described but was not tested in the sources reviewed

muscles.name: Myotomal muscles of the affected root
muscles.effect: Weakness with sustained root compression: L5 (ankle dorsiflexors, extensor hallucis longus, hip abductors) and S1 (plantarflexors, glutei)

muscles.name: Hamstrings and calf
muscles.effect: Protective tightness limits straight leg raise and reflects neural mechanosensitivity rather than true muscle shortening

muscles.name: Deconditioned trunk and hip extensors
muscles.effect: Disuse from prolonged rest or fear of movement reduces trunk endurance and tolerance of lifting

cellular.description: Annular fibres fail, nucleus material contacts the epineurium and dorsal root ganglion. Nucleus cells and extracellular matrix are immunologically exposed [r9].
Pro-inflammatory mediators, including TNF-α, sensitise the nerve root and increase nociceptor firing. Pain is often at its worst in this window (clinical observation).
Macrophages infiltrate and new vessels grow into the herniated tissue, shrinking it. Most resorption occurs within 6 months of conservative treatment [r4,r10].
Nerve root function recovers as compression and inflammation resolve; the annulus heals with fibrous tissue, so the disc is often left narrowed and degenerate.

systems.effect: Mechanical and chemical irritation of the root and dorsal root ganglion produces radicular pain, paraesthesia and, with conduction block, sensory loss, weakness and reflex change [r9]

Central pain-modulating mechanisms and pain cognitions have important roles in persistent disabling low back pain [r6]; in some people pain persists after the herniation has resolved (clinical observation)
The nucleus is immunogenic when exposed outside the annulus; macrophages both amplify inflammation and clear the extruded tissue [r9,r10]

Compression and inflammation are thought to impair intraneural blood flow (largely animal evidence, not tested in the sources reviewed); neovascularisation of the herniated tissue is part of resorption [r10]

Initial high pain intensity, psychological distress and pain at multiple sites increase the risk of persistent disabling low back pain [r6]; fear of movement and catastrophising can prolong disability
Antalgic posture, hip flexor and hamstring guarding and reduced walking tolerance alter loading across the lumbar spine, pelvis and hips

grades.description: Broad-based, symmetrical extension of the annulus beyond the vertebral margins without focal herniation. Often asymptomatic.
grades.prognosis: Resorption in 13.3% in a pooled analysis [r4]; bulges are common in pain-free people [r3]

grades.description: Focal herniation in which the base against the parent disc is wider than any other diameter of the displaced material; the outer annulus is contained.
grades.prognosis: Resorption in 37.5% in a pooled analysis [r4]

grades.description: Displaced material is wider beyond the disc space than at its base (or has lost continuity with the parent disc); the outer annulus is breached. May migrate cranially or caudally.
grades.prognosis: Resorption in 66.9% in a pooled analysis [r4]

grades.description: A free fragment of disc material that has lost continuity with the parent disc and can lie in the canal at a different level.
grades.prognosis: Highest resorption rate in a pooled analysis, 87.8% [r4]; surgery is still considered if neurological deficit progresses or pain is intractable

timeframes.summary: Most radicular pain improves substantially over 6 to 12 weeks, and resorption occurs mainly within 6 months [r4]. In a trial of patients with 6 to 12 weeks of severe sciatica, the probability of perceived recovery at 1 year was 95% in both the early-surgery and conservative arms [r5].

healing.description: Mechanical and chemical nerve root irritation; pain is highest and sleep and sitting are often disturbed
Macrophage-mediated resorption of herniated tissue, mostly within 6 months [r4]; leg pain and neurological signs improve

healing.phase: Remodelling and return to full loading
healing.description: Graded restoration of trunk and hip capacity and lifting tolerance; the annulus heals with fibrous tissue

milestones.label: Walking and light daily activity tolerated
Review point for severe, non-improving leg pain
milestones.note: The Dutch trial enrolled patients with severe sciatica of 6–12 weeks' duration [r5]

milestones.label: Return to usual work (modified duties earlier)
milestones.note: Typical clinical expectation; not a validated criterion

milestones.label: Surgery considered for sciatica persisting 4–12 months
milestones.note: Microdiscectomy gave lower leg pain at 6 months than 6 months of non-operative care in a single-centre trial [r2]

timeframes.returnToSport: Often 6–12 weeks after non-operative recovery and longer after surgery or with a motor deficit, but criteria-based, not time-based. No validated disc-specific return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified, so the criteria below reflect clinical convention.

symptoms: Unilateral leg pain that is equal to or worse than back pain, radiating below the knee in a dermatomal pattern (L5: lateral shin and dorsum of foot; S1: posterior calf and lateral foot)
Pins and needles or numbness in the same distribution
Pain aggravated by sitting, forward bending, coughing, sneezing or straining; eased by lying, walking or standing in a position of comfort
Weakness, such as a foot that slaps or catches (L5) or difficulty rising on the toes (S1)
Night pain and difficulty finding a comfortable position in the acute phase
signs: Antalgic posture, often a lateral shift away from or toward the painful side
Reduced and painful lumbar flexion; extension may be less provocative
Positive straight leg raise or slump test reproducing leg pain
Myotomal weakness (for example ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension, plantarflexion), dermatomal sensory change or a diminished ankle reflex

subjective: Distribution, quality and relative intensity of back versus leg pain, and how far below the knee it extends
Aggravating and easing postures (sitting, flexion, walking, lying) and the response to coughing or straining
Mechanism and time course: a lifting event, repetitive flexion, prolonged sitting, or insidious onset
Neurological symptoms: numbness, weakness, foot drop, change in bladder, bowel or sexual function
Red flag screening: previous cancer, age, steroid use, fever, trauma, unexplained weight loss, night or constant pain [r11]
Yellow flags: distress, fear of movement, belief that rest is needed, work and compensation factors [r6]
Work demands, goals and sleep quality
observation: Antalgic gait, avoidance of sitting or protective standing posture
Foot slap or steppage gait (L5 weakness), reduced push-off (S1)
Loss of normal lumbar lordosis or guarded movement
palpation: Paraspinal tenderness and guarding at the symptomatic level (nonspecific)
Sciatic notch and posterior thigh tenderness (neural mechanosensitivity); tenderness alone does not confirm radiculopathy
rangeOfMotion: Active lumbar flexion, extension and side flexion, noting the effect of each on leg symptoms
Repeated movements and sustained postures to look for centralisation or peripheralisation (directional preference)
Hip range of motion to exclude hip pathology as the pain source
strength: Myotomes L2–S1 bilaterally, including heel and toe walk and single-leg calf raise repetitions to detect subtle S1 weakness
Hip abduction (L5) and ankle dorsiflexion/great toe extension (L4–L5)
neuro: Sacral sensation and bladder, bowel and sexual function screening in any suspected cauda equina syndrome
Document a baseline and re-test myotomes at every visit to detect progression
functional: Walking tolerance and ability to lift an object from the floor

specialTests.name: Straight leg raise (SLR)
specialTests.purpose: Tension on the L5 and S1 nerve roots to identify radiculopathy due to disc herniation
specialTests.procedure: Supine, examiner lifts the extended leg by the heel, stopping at reproduction of leg pain. Dorsiflexing the foot or adding hip adduction increases the load.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of radicular leg pain (not just posterior thigh stretch), commonly between roughly 30° and 70° of hip flexion (clinical convention)

specialTests.name: Crossed (well-leg) SLR
specialTests.purpose: A highly specific sign of disc herniation with root compression
specialTests.procedure: Raise the asymptomatic leg and record whether pain is provoked in the symptomatic leg.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of leg pain on the affected side

specialTests.name: Slump test
specialTests.purpose: Neural tension test that adds trunk and neck flexion to the leg raise
specialTests.procedure: Seated slumped; add neck flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion in sequence until symptoms are reproduced; release neck flexion to see if symptoms ease.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of familiar leg symptoms that changes with neck position
specialTests.sensitivity: 0.84 in one single-examiner study of 75 patients (SLR 0.52 in the same study)

specialTests.name: Neurological screen (myotomes, dermatomes, reflexes)
specialTests.purpose: Identify and track root involvement and progression
specialTests.procedure: Test L2–S1 myotomes, light touch and pinprick, and knee and ankle reflexes bilaterally.
specialTests.positive: Weakness, sensory loss or reduced reflex in the distribution of the suspected root. Used alone, the diagnostic performance of most of these tests was poor, so interpret them together with the history and neural tension signs [r12].

specialTests.name: Femoral nerve stretch (prone knee bend)
specialTests.purpose: Upper lumbar (L2–L4) root involvement, for anterior thigh pain
specialTests.procedure: Prone, passively flex the knee, with or without hip extension.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of anterior thigh pain. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

clinicalRules.name: Cauda equina screen
clinicalRules.description: Ask about saddle sensory change, bladder retention or loss of urinary sensation, faecal incontinence, sexual dysfunction and bilateral leg symptoms or weakness. Any positive item is a same-day emergency referral. Cauda equina syndrome most often follows a large central herniation [r14].

clinicalRules.name: Radicular versus somatic referred pain
clinicalRules.description: Leg pain below the knee in a dermatomal pattern with neural tension or neurological signs supports radiculopathy; non-dermatomal, poorly localised leg pain above the knee is more consistent with somatic referral from the disc, facet or sacroiliac joint.

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric Pain Rating Scale or visual analogue scale for leg and back pain, separately
outcomeMeasures.use: Leg pain was the primary outcome in the surgical trial of persistent sciatica [r2]

outcomeMeasures.name: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
outcomeMeasures.use: Disability measure used as the primary outcome in the oral steroid trial and as a secondary outcome in the surgical trial [r2,r15]

outcomeMeasures.name: Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire
outcomeMeasures.use: Used as a primary outcome in the Dutch surgical trial [r5]

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-Specific Functional Scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Individual goals such as sitting for a work meeting or lifting a child

outcomeMeasures.name: Neurological examination record (myotomes, reflexes, sensation)
outcomeMeasures.use: Serial documentation to detect improvement or progression

imaging.indication: Suspected cauda equina syndrome (emergency); progressive or severe neurological deficit; persistent disabling radicular pain where surgery or an epidural injection is being considered; suspected infection or malignancy. Not for routine early use. Guidelines warn against inappropriately high use of imaging [r16].
imaging.findings: Protrusion, extrusion or sequestration concordant with the symptomatic root, with root displacement or compression in the lateral recess or foramen. Because disc protrusion, bulge and annular fissure appear in pain-free adults [r3], concordance with the clinical level is essential.

imaging.indication: When MRI is contraindicated or bony detail is needed for surgical planning
imaging.findings: Calcified herniation, canal and foraminal dimensions, bony stenosis

imaging.indication: Not helpful for disc herniation; only if fracture, instability or deformity is suspected
imaging.findings: Disc height loss, alignment; the disc and nerve root cannot be seen

differentials.name: Cauda equina syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Bilateral leg symptoms, saddle sensory loss and bladder or bowel dysfunction. Most often caused by a large central herniation [r14]; an emergency, not a differential to be 'ruled out later'.

differentials.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
differentials.distinguishing: Older age, bilateral buttock or leg symptoms provoked by walking and extension and eased by sitting or flexion (neurogenic claudication).

differentials.name: Lumbar facet joint pain
differentials.distinguishing: Back pain with non-dermatomal referral to the buttock or thigh, no neurological signs, no neural tension signs.

differentials.name: Sacroiliac joint pain
differentials.distinguishing: Pain below L5 around the posterior superior iliac spine, a cluster of provocation tests and no neurological signs.

differentials.name: Spondylolisthesis
differentials.distinguishing: Radiographic slip, often with a step on palpation; may coexist with root compression in the foramen.

differentials.name: Deep gluteal syndrome (piriformis/sciatic entrapment)
differentials.distinguishing: Buttock-dominant pain with sitting, local tenderness near the sciatic notch and no lumbar movement dependence.

differentials.name: Proximal hamstring tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Ischial pain on sitting and loaded hip flexion, local palpation reproduces symptoms and neural tests are negative.

differentials.name: Vertebral fracture, infection or malignancy
differentials.distinguishing: Constant or night pain, systemic features, history of cancer, steroid use or significant trauma; see red flags [r11].

redFlags: EMERGENCY: possible cauda equina syndrome. New urinary retention or loss of bladder sensation, faecal incontinence, saddle (perineal) numbness, new sexual dysfunction, or bilateral leg pain or weakness. Send to an emergency department the same day for urgent MRI and surgical review; incomplete cauda equina syndrome (without retention) has a better prognosis if decompressed before it progresses to retention [r14].
Progressive or severe motor deficit (for example foot drop, or loss of one grade of power on serial testing): arrange urgent spinal surgical review, ideally within 24 hours (clinical convention).

Features of fracture, malignancy or infection: history of cancer, age over about 50 with unexplained pain, prolonged corticosteroid use, severe trauma, fever, weight loss, intravenous drug use, or constant night pain. Few individual flags are strongly informative, so look for combinations [r11].
Severe, intractable radicular pain not controlled with appropriate analgesia: seek medical review for analgesic escalation and early specialist opinion.
Bilateral or multi-level neurological signs, or upper motor neuron signs (clonus, extensor plantar): consider myelopathy or central pathology and refer.

management.principles: Most people with a lumbar disc herniation and radiculopathy recover without surgery, so the default plan is education, reassurance about the favourable natural history, staying active within symptom limits, time-limited analgesia and graded exercise [r4,r16]. Guidelines emphasise a biopsychosocial approach, prudent use of imaging and medication, and avoidance of rest [r16]. Referral for a surgical opinion is for progressive or severe motor deficit, suspected cauda equina syndrome, and persistent disabling radicular pain that has not improved with appropriate care. Early surgery speeds the relief of leg pain in severe sciatica but does not change the 1-year outcome [r5]; for sciatica persisting 4 to 12 months, microdiscectomy gave lower leg pain at 6 months than non-operative care [r2]. The decision is therefore a shared one.

medical.name: Simple analgesia and short-course NSAIDs
medical.description: Commonly used for symptom control during the acute phase. A systematic review of drug trials for sciatica found evidence of low to moderate quality, and most pooled estimates did not favour active drugs over placebo, so benefit should not be promised [r17].

medical.name: Short course of oral corticosteroids
medical.description: A 15-day prednisone taper (60, 40 then 20 mg, each for 5 days) gave a modest improvement in function at 3 weeks (ODI 6.4 points) but no significant pain benefit and more adverse events (49.2% vs 23.9%) in one large trial [r15]. Pooled data from 2 earlier trials showed a short-term benefit [r17]. Results conflict and the effect is small.

medical.name: Gabapentinoids (pregabalin)
medical.description: Pregabalin did not reduce leg pain intensity at 8 weeks compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference 0.5, 95% CI −0.2 to 1.2) and caused more adverse events, notably dizziness [r18].

medical.name: Epidural corticosteroid injection
medical.description: Gives a small, short-term reduction in leg pain (mean difference −6.2 on a 0–100 scale) and disability (−3.1); long-term effects were smaller and not significant [r19]. The effect is below the proposed 10–30 point threshold for clinical importance, and the Lancet series flagged inappropriately high use of spinal injections [r16,r19]. Reserve for selected patients with severe radicular pain who want a short-term bridge.

medical.name: Microdiscectomy
medical.description: In severe sciatica of 6–12 weeks, early surgery relieved leg pain faster than prolonged conservative care with surgery if needed, but outcomes at 1 year were similar [r5]. In sciatica lasting 4–12 months, leg pain at 6 months was 2.8 after surgery versus 5.2 after non-operative care (adjusted difference 2.4, 95% CI 1.4–3.4); 34% of the non-operative group crossed over to surgery [r2]. Urgent decompression is indicated for cauda equina syndrome and progressive deficit.

physio.name: Education and reassurance on natural history
physio.description: Explain that most herniations improve, that hurt does not equal harm, and that scan findings are common in pain-free people. Active, individual education that addresses biopsychosocial contributors and self-management is preferred over handing out leaflets [r3,r16,r4].

physio.name: Staying active and graded walking
physio.description: Resume normal activities within symptom limits instead of prolonged rest. Guidelines recommend resumption of normal activities, and the Lancet series lists rest as one of the inappropriately overused responses [r16].

physio.name: Exercise therapy (trunk muscle activation, strengthening and endurance)
physio.description: The 2021 JOSPT guideline states that physical therapists may use exercise, including trunk strengthening and endurance and specific trunk muscle activation, to reduce pain and disability in acute low back pain with leg pain [r20]. The evidence relates to low back pain with leg pain rather than imaging-confirmed herniation.

physio.name: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy (directional preference exercises)
physio.description: Repeated movements to find a direction that centralises or reduces leg symptoms, then prescribing that direction (often extension) and avoiding the provocative direction. The JOSPT guideline says physical therapists can use MDT for acute low back pain; the evidence is not specific to radiculopathy [r20].

physio.name: Neural mobilisation (sliders)
physio.description: Gentle sliders, not tensioners, once irritability is low. The guideline says physical therapists may use neural mobilisation with other treatments for short-term benefit in chronic low back pain with leg pain; there is no direct evidence for acute radiculopathy in the sources reviewed [r20].

physio.name: Joint mobilisation or manipulation and soft tissue work
physio.description: The guideline recommends thrust or non-thrust mobilisation for acute low back pain and says it may be used in chronic low back pain with leg pain. Use for symptom relief to enable movement and avoid forceful end-range techniques into a clearly irritable radiculopathy [r20].

physio.name: Mechanical traction
physio.description: The guideline recommends against mechanical traction for chronic low back pain with leg pain because of a lack of benefit when added to other interventions. Acute radiculopathy was not addressed separately [r20].

physio.name: Psychosocial screening and pacing
physio.description: Identify distress, fear of movement and multi-site pain, which increase the risk of persistent disabling low back pain, and address them with graded exposure and activity pacing [r6,r16].

physio.name: Post-discectomy rehabilitation
physio.description: The guideline says physical therapists can use general exercise for low back pain after lumbar spine surgery and may use general education covering postsurgical precautions and resuming activity; follow the surgeon's protocol [r20].

education: Most disc herniations improve on their own over weeks to months, and the herniated material often shrinks. Your nerve is irritated, not permanently damaged.
A scan finding does not equal damage. Many pain-free people have bulges and protrusions, so we treat you and not the picture.
Staying gently active is safer and faster than bed rest. Walk in short, frequent bouts and change position often; avoid sitting for long periods early on.
Leg pain usually reduces before back pain, and numbness can lag behind. The leg pain moving higher up the leg (centralising) is a good sign.
Contact us or go to an emergency department the same day if you develop numbness around the genitals or buttocks, difficulty passing urine, loss of bowel control, or weakness that is getting worse.
Surgery is an option if severe leg pain does not settle, but it speeds recovery rather than changing the final outcome for most people.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and driven by the leg-pain and neurological trajectory rather than the calendar. Start with education, walking and a movement direction that reduces leg symptoms; then rebuild trunk and hip control, then strength and lifting capacity, then job- or sport-specific exposure, including graded reintroduction of loaded flexion that the person fears [r16,r20]. Dosages below are typical clinical conventions, not trial-derived. The 2021 JOSPT guideline supports exercise for low back pain with leg pain but does not specify a regimen for disc herniation [r20]. Stop any exercise that peripheralises symptoms (moves them further down the leg) or worsens neurological signs, and re-check the neurological status at each visit.

stages.name: Settle & stay active
goals: Leg pain trending down and sleep improving
Walking 20 minutes without increasing leg symptoms
Understand the favourable natural history and what to avoid early
Find a movement or posture that reduces or centralises leg symptoms
precautions: Refer the same day for any new bladder, bowel or saddle symptoms, bilateral symptoms or rapidly progressing weakness [r14]
Do not repeat a movement that peripheralises leg pain
Avoid prolonged slouched sitting and repeated loaded end-range flexion early (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Short, frequent walks
exercises.dosage: 5–15 minutes, 3–6 times a day, as symptoms allow, adding about 10% every few days (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Walk tall, relaxed arm swing; stop before leg pain builds

exercises.name: Directional preference exercise (for example prone lying then prone press-up if it centralises)
exercises.dosage: 8–10 repetitions every 2 hours while awake, only if leg symptoms centralise or reduce (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Relax the buttocks and let the back sag; stop if pain moves further down the leg

exercises.name: Cat–camel in pain-free range
exercises.dosage: 2 sets of 10 slow repetitions, 3–4 times a day (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Seated slump slider (neural glide)
exercises.dosage: 1–2 sets of 10 gentle repetitions once or twice daily, only if leg symptoms do not linger afterwards (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Slide, do not tension: knee extends as the head lowers, then the reverse

exercises.name: Supine abdominal bracing with breathing
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions of 5-second holds, twice daily (clinical convention)

progressionCriteria: Resting leg pain 4/10 or less and sleep not routinely disturbed
Walking 20 minutes tolerated without provoking leg symptoms
Neurological signs stable or improving on repeat examination
Able to repeat the preferred movement without peripheralisation

stages.name: Restore movement & trunk control
goals: Normal pain-free lumbar movement without leg symptoms
Segmental and global trunk control in neutral
Sitting tolerance of at least 45–60 minutes
precautions: Progress a new load only if leg symptoms are no worse after 24 hours (clinical convention)
Keep neural sliders gentle; do not tension the nerve

exercises.name: Bird-dog
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per side with 5-second holds, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Level pelvis; reach long rather than high

exercises.name: Dead bug
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per side, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Keep the low back flat on the floor as the limbs move

exercises.name: Side plank (knees, then feet)
exercises.dosage: 3 holds of 15–30 seconds per side, building to 45 seconds (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Stack the hips, lift the waist off the floor

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 10 repetitions with a 3-second hold, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels; ribs down, avoid arching the low back

exercises.name: Hip hinge pattern with dowel or light weight
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 10 repetitions, 3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Push the hips back, keep the dowel in contact with head, upper back and sacrum

progressionCriteria: Leg pain 2/10 or less during daily tasks
Normal lumbar flexion and extension without peripheralisation
Side plank at least 30 seconds each side with similar technique (clinical convention)

stages.name: Build strength & lifting capacity
goals: Restore hip and trunk strength and endurance
Lift from the floor with good technique at progressive loads
Rebuild confidence in loaded forward bending
precautions: Increase load or repetitions by roughly 5–10% a week, one variable at a time (clinical convention)
Hold back if radicular symptoms return or progress

exercises.name: Hip thrust
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8–10 repetitions at a load that leaves 2–3 repetitions in reserve, 2–3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Posterior pelvic tilt at the top; chin tucked

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift or trap-bar deadlift
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 6–8 repetitions, progressive load, 2 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Hinge from the hips, lats on, bar close to the legs

exercises.name: Goblet squat
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8–10 repetitions, 2 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Knees track over the toes, trunk upright

exercises.name: Forearm plank
exercises.dosage: 3 holds of 30–45 seconds, 3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Straight line from head to heels; squeeze the glutes

exercises.name: Farmer carry
exercises.dosage: 3 carries of 20–30 metres at a challenging load, 2 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Walk tall, avoid leaning to the loaded side

progressionCriteria: No leg pain provoked by training loads
Deadlift or squat with a load meaningful for the person's work or sport and technique maintained
Plank 45 seconds or more and side plank symmetry within about 10% (clinical convention)
Fear of loaded forward bending low (for example Fear-Avoidance Beliefs or the person's own rating)

stages.name: Return to work & sport
goals: Meet the physical demands of the job or sport
Graded exposure to repeated loaded flexion in a controlled way
precautions: Return to full duties through graded steps, not in a single step
If there was a motor deficit or surgery, follow the surgeon's protocol and confirm clearance

exercises.name: Graded floor-to-waist box lift
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 5–8 repetitions, starting at roughly half the work load and increasing weekly (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Choose the technique that suits the person; neither squat nor stoop is mandatory, but progress to the load and posture the job needs

exercises.name: Squat lift from the floor with carry
exercises.dosage: 4 sets of 6 repetitions at work-simulation loads, 2–3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Load close to the body; exhale on the effort

exercises.name: Anti-rotation and rotational power drills
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 per side, building speed progressively (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Control the pelvis; rotate through the hips and thoracic spine

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills (for example running, throwing or hop progressions)
exercises.dosage: Build from a fraction of usual volume in steps of roughly 10–20% a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Stop the session if leg symptoms return

progressionCriteria: Full job or sport demands completed without leg symptoms
Written self-management and flare-up plan agreed

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria specific to lumbar disc herniation were identified in the sources reviewed; the criteria below reflect clinical convention
Leg pain absent or 1–2/10 during work and sport tasks, with no peripheralisation
Neurological examination stable or normal; motor power equal to the other side or plateaued (agree with the surgeon after surgery)
Full lumbar range of movement without leg symptoms
Trunk and hip endurance and strength adequate for the demands (side plank symmetry within about 10%)
Able to perform repeated lifts at the load and posture required for the job or sport
Low fear of loaded forward bending and a flare-up plan in place
tests: Slump and SLR repeated and compared with baseline
Repeated floor-to-waist lift at 50–75% of work load for 10 repetitions (clinical convention)
Single-leg squat and hip hinge movement quality
Oswestry Disability Index or Patient-Specific Functional Scale against the person's goal

prognosis: The prognosis is favourable. In patients with 6 to 12 weeks of severe sciatica, the probability of perceived recovery at 1 year was 95% whether they had early surgery or conservative care, although 39% of the conservative group went on to surgery after a mean of 18.7 weeks [r5]. Resorption of herniated tissue occurs in about 70% of conservatively treated herniations (higher with extrusion and sequestration) and mostly within 6 months [r4]. Resorption is less likely when Modic changes are present [r10]. When sciatica has already persisted for 4 to 12 months, 34% of those given non-operative care crossed over to surgery by a median of 11 months, and leg pain at 6 months was lower after microdiscectomy [r2]. Persistent disabling low back pain is more likely with high initial pain intensity, psychological distress and pain at multiple sites [r6]. Repeat herniation after surgery is uncommon in trial data (1 repeat surgery among the 64 operated patients in one trial) but the figures are small [r2].
prevention: No intervention has been shown to prevent disc herniation specifically; the strategies below are extrapolated from laboratory and general low back pain evidence.
Vary posture and avoid repetitive end-range flexion under load for long periods, because repeated flexion with compression produced herniation in a laboratory model [r7].
Build and maintain general fitness and trunk and hip strength, in line with guideline emphasis on exercise and activity [r16].
Address modifiable risk factors for low back pain: smoking, obesity and physically demanding work without recovery [r6].
clinicalPearls: Match the scan to the leg. Dermatomal pain below the knee, a neural tension sign and a concordant MRI level support radiculopathy; protrusions appear in 29–43% of pain-free adults and symptom severity correlates poorly with herniation size [r3,r9].
Larger can resolve better: extruded and sequestered fragments resorb more often (66.9–87.8%) than contained protrusions (37.5%) [r4]. Reassure, but keep checking motor function.

A negative SLR does not exclude a herniation. SLR is sensitive in surgical samples (0.92) but poorly specific (0.28), and a positive crossed SLR is the most specific sign (0.90) [r12]. The slump test had higher sensitivity than SLR in one small single-examiner study [r13].
Progression, not the initial deficit, drives urgency. Re-test myotomes and reflexes at every early visit and document them.

Ask every person with leg pain about bladder, bowel and saddle sensation and record the answers. Incomplete cauda equina syndrome with a better prognosis may be missed if the questions are not asked [r14].
Use the leg-pain response as the compass: if a direction or posture centralises or reduces leg pain, load that direction; if it peripheralises, stop and change course.

animation.title: How a lumbar disc herniation happens

captions.text: A worker repeatedly lifts a box from the floor with a bent, stooped back.
Each repetition flexes the lumbar spine while the disc carries the weight of the trunk and the load.
At end-range flexion under load, the back of the disc is stretched and the nucleus is squeezed backwards.
Cumulative loading, not one lift, usually fissures the annulus. The last lift is the one that gives.
Pain starts in the back; leg pain follows as the herniated material reaches a nerve root.
Zooming into the L4–5 disc, shown as a horizontal slice viewed from below.
In this slice the nucleus sits inside the annulus, with the thecal sac and L5 roots behind the disc.
With the spine flexed under load, the nucleus is pushed toward the weaker back of the disc.
Repeated loading fissures the posterior annulus, creating a path for the nucleus to track along.
The disc bulges out to one side, beside the midline, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is thinnest.
The nucleus can break through the outer annulus (extrusion) and press on the traversing root.
Compression plus inflammatory chemicals from the nucleus fire the nerve, causing leg-dominant pain.
The paraspinal muscles guard reflexively. A large central herniation can instead compress the cauda equina: an emergency.
A healthy disc: a hydrated nucleus held within concentric annular lamellae.
Loading squeezes the nucleus and tensions the posterior annulus.
Repeated loading fatigues the lamellae and annular fissures form.
Nucleus material migrates along the fissure toward the outer annulus.
The nucleus herniates through the annulus into the canal.
Exposed nucleus triggers an inflammatory reaction that sensitises the nerve root.
Macrophages and new vessels clear the herniated tissue, and in most people it shrinks over months.
